propositions.text: Teva Canada Limited moves to strike Gilead's statement of claim for insufficient material facts for past infringement and quia timet claim
propositions.quote: Teva Canada Limited brings this motion to strike the statement of claim of the plaintiffs Gilead Sciences Inc., Gilead Sciences Canada Inc. and Bristol-Myers Squibb and Gilead Sciences LLC (collectively “Gilead”) on the basis that it fails to plead sufficient material facts to support an action for past infringement or to properly support a quia timet claim.

propositions.text: Gilead argues its pleaded facts are sufficient or should be allowed to amend with discovery information from separate action
propositions.quote: Gilead argues that the facts it has pleaded are sufficient but , if not, that it should be given an opportunity to amend to plead further material facts, including facts that have been disclosed to it in the course of discovery in a separate action involving Gilead Sciences Inc. and Teva.

propositions.text: Gilead seeks relief from implied undertaking rule to use discovery information for this litigation
propositions.quote: In order to do this, Gilead Sciences Inc. has sought to be relieved of the implied undertaking rule, pursuant to which it is prevented from using information obtained on discovery for any other litigation or purpose.

paragraphs.summary: Teva moves to strike Gilead's claim for insufficient facts; Gilead argues sufficiency or amendment and seeks relief from implied undertaking rule to use discovery.

propositions.text: Gilead should be relieved of the implied undertaking rule
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that Gilead should be relieved of the implied undertaking rule.

propositions.text: Gilead's current statement of claim fails to plead sufficient facts for past or current infringement and proposed amendments should not be permitted
propositions.quote: I have also concluded that Gilead’s statement of claim, as it currently exists, fails to set out sufficient material facts to support an action for past or current infringement and that none of the amendments proposed by Gilead should be permitted in an attempt to cure that defect.

propositions.text: Current statement of claim fails to allege sufficient facts for quia timet claim but proposed amendments plus further particulars would suffice and should be allowed
propositions.quote: With respect to the quia timet claim, the statement of claim, as currently framed, also fails to allege sufficient material facts but I am satisfied that the amendments proposed in Gilead’s motion record, combined with further particulars as to the extent of the losses it would suffer, would be sufficient to sustain a quia timet claim, and that Gilead should be given an opportunity to make those amendments.

paragraphs.summary: Court grants relief from implied undertaking rule; strikes claim for past/current infringement; allows amendments for quia timet claim.

propositions.text: Teva designated discovery information as confidential under protective order which did not authorize filing under seal without court approval
propositions.quote: The discovery information at issue had been designated by Teva as confidential pursuant to a protective order issued in the relevant proceeding. That protective order governed the manner in which the parties were to treat information exchanged between them, but did not authorize them to file information under seal without first demonstrating to the Court that the information merits the protection of a confidentiality order.

propositions.text: Teva moved for confidentiality order for discovery information
propositions.quote: Teva has now made a motion for a confidentiality order in respect of the discovery information at issue.

propositions.text: If Gilead's motion were dismissed, implied undertaking rule alone would justify confidentiality order
propositions.quote: The need to uphold and enforce the implied undertaking rule would, by itself, justify the issuance of a confidentiality order if Gilead’s motion were dismissed.

propositions.text: If Gilead relieved of implied undertaking rule, Teva's evidence insufficient to support confidentiality order
propositions.quote: However, if Gilead were relieved of the implied undertaking rule, the evidence tendered by Teva on its motion is insufficient to support a confidentiality order.

propositions.text: Teva's evidence only shows it treated information as confidential but does not show disclosure would cause serious harm
propositions.quote: The evidence demonstrates only that Teva has always treated the information as confidential; it falls short of establishing that disclosure would likely cause serious harm to Teva.

propositions.text: Teva abandoned motion for confidentiality order
propositions.quote: Teva has now abandoned its motion for a confidentiality order,

propositions.text: Discovery information remains under seal until all appeals of order relieving Gilead from implied undertaking rule are exhausted
propositions.quote: the discovery information shall remain under seal until all avenues of appeal of that order have been exhausted.

propositions.text: Court avoids discussing specifics of discovery information to protect confidentiality
propositions.quote: I have avoided discussing in these reasons the specifics of the discovery information at issue.

propositions.text: General nature of discovery information is sufficient to understand reasons
propositions.quote: It is sufficient, for these reasons to be intelligible, that the general nature of the information be disclosed.

paragraphs.summary: Teva designated discovery info confidential; motion for confidentiality order abandoned; info remains sealed pending appeals; court avoids specifics.

propositions.text: This action involves Canadian patents 059 and 619 owned by Gilead covering TDF and TD
propositions.quote: This action is part of a series of proceedings involving Canadian patents number 2,298,059 (the “059 Patent”) and 2,261,619 (the “619 Patent”), owned by Gilead Sciences, Inc. and covering, respectively, the fumarate salt of tenofovir disoproxil (“TDF”) and tenofovir disoproxil (“TD”) itself.

propositions.text: These antiviral drugs marketed in Canada by Gilead Canada under trademarks TRUVADA, ATRIPLA and VIREAD
propositions.quote: These antiviral drugs have been marketed in Canada by Gilead Sciences Canada, Inc. under the trademarks TRUVADA, ATRIPLA and VIREAD.

propositions.text: 059 Patent expires July 23, 2018; 619 Patent expires July 25, 2017
propositions.quote: The 059 Patent will expire on July 23, 2018, while the 619 Patent will expire on July 25, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The action concerns Gilead's Canadian patents 059 and 619 covering TDF and TD, marketed under TRUVADA, ATRIPLA, VIREAD, expiring 2017-2018.

propositions.text: In 2011-2012, Teva served Notices of Allegation alleging invalidity of patents but not non-infringement
propositions.quote: In late 2011 and 2012, Teva served on Gilead Notices of Allegation for products containing TDF which it compared to TRUVADA, ATRIPLA and VIREAD, against which both patents were listed. The Notices of Allegation alleged only the invalidity of the patents; they did not contain allegations of non-infringement.

propositions.text: Gilead responded by commencing applications under PM(NOC) Regulations to prohibit Minister from issuing NOCs to Teva until patent expiry
propositions.quote: Gilead responded by commencing applications under the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations, SOR/93-133 for orders prohibiting the Minister of Health from issuing Notices of Compliance to Teva for these products until the expiration of the 059 and 619 Patents

paragraphs.summary: Teva alleged patent invalidity in Notices of Allegation; Gilead sought orders to prohibit Minister issuing NOCs to Teva until patent expiry.

propositions.text: While prohibition proceedings pending, Teva filed action T-1529-12 seeking declaration patents invalid and alleging intent to import, make, use and sell TDF products
propositions.quote: While the prohibition proceedings were still pending, Teva, in August 2012, served and filed a statement of claim in Court file T-1529-12, seeking a declaration that the 619 and 059 Patents are invalid, void and of no force and effect. That action does not make any allegation or seek any declaration with respect to the non-infringement of the patents, but it does allege that Teva Canada is an interested party because it wishes to import, make, use and sell in Canada TDF or products containing TDF.

propositions.text: Discovery transcripts Gilead seeks to use were from T-1529-12 action in October 2013, after prohibition hearing but before judgment
propositions.quote: The discovery transcripts that Gilead seeks to use were constituted in that impeachment action in October 2013, after the hearing of the prohibition proceedings, but before a judgment was rendered.

paragraphs.summary: Teva filed action T-1529-12 alleging patent invalidity and intent to market TDF; discovery transcripts sought by Gilead were from that action.

propositions.text: On Dec 20, 2013, Court prohibited Minister from issuing NOC to Teva until 619 Patent expiry but dismissed applications re 059 Patent
propositions.quote: On December 20, 2013, this Court granted an order prohibiting the Minister of Health from issuing an NOC to Teva until after the expiry of the 619 Patent in each of Court files T-8-12, T-280-12 and T-1708-12, but dismissed all applications in respect of the 059 Patent.

propositions.text: Minister could issue NOCs to Teva as early as July 25, 2017, the 619 Patent expiry date
propositions.quote: As a result, the Minister of Health could issue NOCs to Teva as early as July 25, 2017, the date of expiry of the 619 Patent.

paragraphs.summary: Court prohibited Minister issuing NOC to Teva until 619 Patent expiry but dismissed 059 Patent applications; NOCs could issue from July 25, 2017.

propositions.text: Teva continued impeachment action T-1529-12 for both patents; trial set for March 2, 2015; discoveries and expert reports exchanged in 2014
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding this decision, Teva continued to prosecute its impeachment action in Court file T-1529-12 in respect of both patents. The trial was set to begin on March 2, 2015. Discoveries were completed and expert reports were exchanged in 2014.

propositions.text: On Dec 17, 2014, Teva served notice of discontinuance of T-1529-12 action only for 059 Patent; pleadings not amended
propositions.quote: On December 17, 2014, less than three months prior to the expected start of the trial, Teva served and filed a notice of discontinuance of the action in T-1529-12, but in relation to the 059 Patent only. The pleadings themselves were not amended.

paragraphs.summary: Teva continued impeachment action with trial set for March 2015; discontinued 059 Patent claim in Dec 2014 without amending pleadings.

propositions.text: Trial adjourned from March 2, 2015 to November 28, 2016 due to serious illness of Teva's expert witness
propositions.quote: Due to the unforeseen and serious illness of one of Teva’s main expert witnesses in mid-February 2015, the trial, initially scheduled to begin on March 2, 2015, had to be adjourned. It is now scheduled to take place beginning on November 28, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: Trial adjourned to November 28, 2016 due to serious illness of Teva's expert witness.

propositions.text: On Nov 9, 2015, Gilead commenced present action seeking declaration of past and future infringement of 059 Patent
propositions.quote: On November 9, 2015, Gilead instituted the present action, seeking a declaration that Teva has in the past and will in the future infringe the 059 Patent.

propositions.text: Teva demanded particulars of allegations of past, current and future infringement and intent to market from July 25, 2017
propositions.quote: Teva immediately demanded particulars in respect, inter alia, of the allegations of past and current infringement, as well as the allegations that Teva intends to come to market with products containing TDF as early as July 25, 2017.

propositions.text: Gilead declined to provide further particulars, prompting Teva's motion to strike
propositions.quote: In response, Gilead declined to provide further particulars of the circumstances of the past, current or future infringement, prompting Teva to bring the present motion to strike.

paragraphs.summary: Gilead sued for past and future infringement; Teva demanded particulars; Gilead declined; Teva moved to strike claim.

propositions.text: Gilead filed motion to consolidate present action with T-1529-12 for joint hearing in Nov 2016, pending survival of motion to strike
propositions.quote: Gilead has, in parallel, also filed a motion to consolidate this action with the action in T-1529-12 so that they be heard together in November 2016. That motion is scheduled to be heard shortly by the Judge designated to preside over the trial in Court file T-1529-12, if Gilead’s action survives this motion to strike.

paragraphs.summary: Gilead moved to consolidate this action with T-1529-12 for joint hearing in Nov 2016, if claim survives motion to strike.

propositions.text: Gilead alleges Teva intends to import, make, use and sell TDF products before 059 Patent expiry, as early as July 25, 2017
propositions.quote: Gilead has in this matter made a general allegation to the effect that Teva intends to and will import, make, use and sell in Canada products containing TDF prior to the expiry of the 059 Patent, and as early as July 25, 2017.

propositions.text: Teva's motion to strike challenges Gilead to plead specific material facts supporting this allegation or face striking
propositions.quote: Teva, by its motion to strike, has put Gilead to the task of pleading the specific material facts upon which this allegation is based or see its statement of claim struck.

propositions.text: Gilead wishes to use discovery transcript from T-1529-12 action to meet this challenge
propositions.quote: Gilead wishes to use a portion of the discovery transcript constituted in the T-1529-12 impeachment action to meet that challenge.

paragraphs.summary: Gilead alleges Teva will market TDF before patent expiry; Teva demands specific facts; Gilead seeks to use discovery from T-1529-12 to support claim.

propositions.text: Teva alleges in T-1529-12 it is interested person wishing to import, make, use and sell TDF and must impeach patents or succeed under PM(NOC) Regulations to sell before expiry
propositions.quote: Teva specifically alleges in the T-1529-12 impeachment action that it is an interested person because it wishes to import, make, use and sell in Canada TDF or products containing TDF and because it must “either successfully impeach the relevant claims and/or succeed in an application under the PM (NOC) Regulations in order to sell the Teva Products prior to the expiry of the 619 Patent and the 059 Patent”.

propositions.text: Discoveries in T-1529-12 addressed Teva's intentions and actions including approvability status of NOC submissions
propositions.quote: The discoveries in that action were conducted at a time where the 059 Patent was still very much at issue. The examination on discovery addressed Teva’s intentions, as well as what it had done to act on those intentions, including the approvability status of its submissions for NOCs with the Minister of Health.

paragraphs.summary: Teva alleged in T-1529-12 it intends to market TDF and must impeach patents or succeed under regulations; discovery addressed these intentions and actions.

propositions.text: Implied undertaking rule prevents use of discovery information outside litigation in which it was disclosed to protect privacy and encourage candid discovery
propositions.quote: The implied undertaking of confidentiality prevents the use of information obtained in discovery from being used other than in the litigation in which it was disclosed. The rationale behind the rule is twofold. First, the rule exists to protect the privacy interests of the persons being examined in the face of compulsory discovery, achieving a balance between the public interest in getting at the truth in a civil action and the preservation of the rights of the “reluctant participants” in litigation, by ensuring that the invasion of privacy is limited to satisfying the sole purpose of that litigation. Second, the rule encourages parties to provide a more complete and candid discovery, again, furthering the interest of justice by giving them some assurance that the documents and answers will not be used for a purpose collateral or ulterior to the proceedings (Juman v Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, at paras 23 to 26; Sanofi-Aventis Canada Inc. et al v Apotex Inc. 2008 FC 320, at paras 16 and 17).

propositions.text: Court may relieve persons from implied undertaking rule if in interest of justice
propositions.quote: The rule is not however absolute and the Court retains the power to relieve persons of the obligation where it is in the interest of justice to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The implied undertaking rule restricts use of discovery info to original litigation to protect privacy and encourage candor; court may relieve rule in interest of justice.

propositions.text: Juman v Doucette requires applicant to show public interest outweighing values protected by implied undertaking rule on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court decision in Juman v Doucette, above, establishes at paragraph 32 that an application for relief “requires an applicant to demonstrate to the court on the balance of probabilities the existence of a public interest of greater weight than the values the implied undertaking rule is designed to protect”.

propositions.text: Teva argues Juman sets higher standard than previously applied
propositions.quote: Teva argues that this statement sets a higher standard than that which had been previously applied by the courts.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Teva's interpretation of Juman; Supreme Court recognizes existing provincial rules and flexible categories of superior public interests
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with this interpretation. In the discussion that follows paragraph 32, the Supreme Court explicitly recognizes existing provincial rules of practice as aptly codifying the common law on the issue and goes on to cite some case law which it considers provides useful guidance to the exercise of the court’s discretion. At paragraph 38, the Supreme Court expressly states that the categories of superior public interests it discusses are not meant to be fixed.

paragraphs.summary: Juman requires showing public interest outweighs implied undertaking values; Teva argues higher standard; court disagrees and notes flexibility.

propositions.text: Superior public interest category includes where deponent gave contradictory testimony in different proceedings
propositions.quote: One of the categories of superior public interests recognized by the Supreme Court in Juman is where the deponent has given contradictory testimony about the same matters in successive or different proceedings.

propositions.text: Supreme Court reasons implied undertaking should not allow witness to tailor evidence to suit needs in each proceeding
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court reasons that “[a]n undertaking implied by the Court (or imposed by the legislature) to make civil litigation more effective should not permit the witness to play games with the administration of justice […] Any other outcome would allow a person accused of an offense [w]ith impunity [to] taylor his evidence to suit his needs in each particular proceeding”.

propositions.text: Gilead argues similar superior public interest applies here involving Teva's litigation positions rather than individual witness testimony
propositions.quote: Gilead essentially argues that the same superior public interest is at play here, but involving the litigation positions taken by Teva as a party, rather than the testimony given by an individual witness or accused.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Gilead that superior public interest applies to Teva's litigation positions
propositions.quote: I agree.

paragraphs.summary: Superior public interest includes preventing contradictory testimony; Gilead argues it applies to Teva's litigation positions; court agrees.

propositions.text: Teva publicly alleged intent to market TDF before patent expiry in T-1529-12 and disclosed supporting facts in discovery to advance its interests
propositions.quote: Where it suited its purpose, as plaintiff in the T-1529-12 impeachment action, Teva publicly described itself as an interested party on the basis of express allegations of an intent to come to market with products containing TDF prior to the expiry of the subject patents. It is fair to say that any facts that may have been disclosed on discovery by Teva to flesh out or support these allegations were proffered to advance Teva’s own interests in that litigation.

propositions.text: Teva now argues Gilead cannot meet requirements for quia timet action or allege intent to launch TDF products and has no material facts showing intent or capability
propositions.quote: Now that it is sued by at least one of the same parties on the basis of that very same stated intention, with full knowledge of the facts and testimony it has previously given to support those allegations, Teva takes the position that Gilead “cannot meet the requirements for a quia timet action”, “have no basis upon which to allege that Teva will launch TDF products”, “are only speculating that Teva will launch or intends to launch TDF products”, “have no knowledge as to whether Teva will or will even be capable to carry out the alleged activities” and “have no material facts showing that Teva intends to and can in fact launch infringing product if and when it receives regulatory approval”.

propositions.text: Gilead says Teva's position relies on implied undertaking rule; discovery evidence would show Teva's admissions supporting intent to launch TDF
propositions.quote: According to Gilead, the position taken by Teva can only be sustained by reliance on the implied undertaking rule: Had the evidence Teva gave on discovery been adduced at trial or not been protected by the implied undertaking rule, it would show ample basis, in the form of admissions by Teva, to conclude that it can and will launch TDF products prior to the expiration of the 059 Patent.

paragraphs.summary: Teva publicly alleged intent to market TDF and disclosed facts; now denies Gilead's claim citing lack of facts; Gilead says this relies on implied undertaking rule.

propositions.text: Circumstances differ from Juman and others where discovery evidence was reluctantly provided and revealed unknown facts
propositions.quote: The circumstances here are quite different from those in Juman, Carbone v De La Rocha, [1993] OJ No 1113 or Goodman v Rossi [1995] OJ No 1906. In those cases, the discovery evidence sought to be used against the disclosing witness was reluctantly provided, and revealed facts that would never have come to the knowledge of the requesting party outside the context of discovery and the compulsion or encouragement to full and frank disclosure the implied undertaking rule seeks to promote.

propositions.text: Here, discovery evidence supported factual allegation voluntarily made by Teva for its own interest and was not harmful to Teva's case
propositions.quote: Here, the discovery evidence went to support a factual allegation voluntarily and publicly made by Teva for its own interest. The information was not of a nature to hurt Teva’s case or support Gilead’s defence;

propositions.text: Had Teva refused to answer discovery on status as interested person, sanction likely would be inability to introduce trial evidence without leave, not compulsion or striking pleadings
propositions.quote: had Teva refused to answer discovery questions pertaining to its status as an interested person, the sanction would likely have been, not compulsion or the striking of its pleadings, but the inability to introduce trial evidence establishing that information without leave of the court, pursuant to rule 248.

propositions.text: Teva requested Gilead admit its status as interested person and served 'will say' statement that Teva will come to market immediately upon NOC receipt
propositions.quote: Indeed, in preparation for the trial, Teva formally requested that Gilead admit its status as an interested person and served on Gilead a “will say” statement to the effect that a representative of Teva would testify that “Teva will come to market immediately upon receipt of a Notice of Compliance from Health Canada for the Teva Products.”

paragraphs.summary: Unlike prior cases, Teva voluntarily disclosed discovery evidence supporting its allegations and requested Gilead admit its interested person status.

propositions.text: Discovery evidence likely would have been disclosed by Teva even without implied undertaking rule as it advanced its case
propositions.quote: The discovery evidence at issue is the kind of information which Teva would most likely have disclosed to Gilead even in the absence of the implied undertaking rule, as it needed to do so to advance its own case.

propositions.text: Teva confirmed intention to adduce similar evidence at trial in will-say statement
propositions.quote: Teva confirmed, in its will-say statement, its intention to adduce evidence of that same nature at the trial.

propositions.text: Upholding implied undertaking rule would allow Teva to delay public disclosure and use it to play games with justice by asserting intent in one proceeding and denying basis in another
propositions.quote: Upholding the implied undertaking rule in the circumstances would merely permit Teva to delay the public disclosure of information it has continuously intended to use at trial, and by doing so, delay Gilead’s ability to use it. Teva is using the implied undertaking rule to play games with the administration of justice, by asserting in one proceeding that it will lead evidence at trial of its intent to market TDF products in Canada prior to the expiration of the 619 and 059 patents, while at the same time alleging that there exists no factual basis to support that same allegation when made by Gilead.

propositions.text: Public interest in preventing misuse of implied undertaking rule outweighs values it protects because Teva was not a reluctant litigant needing protection
propositions.quote: I find that the public interest in preventing the use of the implied undertaking rule for this purpose must, in this case, be given greater weight than the values the implied undertaking rule is designed to protect, in part because in giving the discovery evidence at issue, it is clear that Teva was not a “reluctant litigant” giving evidence by compulsion or out of a duty to give complete and candid discovery, and not in need of the protection offered by the implied undertaking.

paragraphs.summary: Teva would have disclosed evidence anyway; upholding implied undertaking would let Teva delay disclosure and play games; public interest favors relief from rule.

propositions.text: Juman recognizes leave to use discovery in another action with same or similar parties and issues will generally be granted as prejudice is virtually nonexistent
propositions.quote: I further note that the Supreme Court in Juman recognized at paragraph 35 that “where discovery material in one action is sought to be used in another action with the same or similar parties and the same or similar issues, the prejudice to the examinee is virtually nonexistent and leave will generally be granted”.

propositions.text: Present action includes additional parties but they are similar parties claiming under patentee; causes of action are related; issue of Teva's intent to market is the same
propositions.quote: While the present action includes additional parties, such as Gilead affiliates and Bristol-Myers Squibb, these additional plaintiffs claim under the patentee pursuant to section 55 of the Patent Act, RCS 1985, c P-4 and are therefore “similar parties”. And while the present action is for patent infringement rather than impeachment, and therefore based on different causes of action, these causes of action are clearly related. More importantly, the narrow issue of whether Teva intends to and will come to market prior to the expiration of the 619 and/or 059 Patents is not just similar, it is the same.

propositions.text: Teva cannot claim actions are distinct because current action concerns only 059 Patent while T-1529-12 no longer concerns that patent; 059 Patent was at issue when discovery given
propositions.quote: Teva cannot claim that they are distinct merely because the current action concerns only the 059 Patent while the T-1529-12 action no longer concern that Patent: At the time discovery was given, the 059 Patent was directly at issue.

paragraphs.summary: Juman allows use of discovery in related actions with similar parties; here parties and issues are similar and discovery was given when 059 Patent was at issue.

propositions.text: Gilead's statement of claim only vaguely alleges past or current infringement without sufficient material facts.
propositions.quote: Gilead’s statement of claim, as currently written, only alleges past or current infringement in the vaguest and broadest of terms

propositions.text: Teva sought particulars of facts supporting Gilead's allegations but was refused.
propositions.quote: Teva promptly sought but was refused particulars of the facts upon which Gilead relies to support these allegations

propositions.text: Infringement actions lacking sufficient material facts and relying on bald conclusions or regulatory approval constitute abuse of process and should be struck.
propositions.quote: an infringement action that fails to set out sufficient material facts by which a defendant is alleged to have infringed a patent and relies solely on bald conclusions of infringement or on the mere fact that a defendant pharmaceutical company has sought regulatory approval to market a medicine constitutes an abuse of process and should be struck

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Gilead's infringement allegations vague and insufficient, notes Teva's refused request for particulars, and cites case law that such claims are an abuse of process.

propositions.text: Gilead's allegations of past or current infringement must be struck as plain and obvious.
propositions.quote: it is plain and obvious that Gilead’s allegations of past or current infringement must be struck

propositions.text: Whether Gilead's proposed amendments to cure the defect should be allowed.
propositions.quote: The question then becomes whether the amendments proposed by Gilead to cure this defect should be allowed

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Gilead's past or current infringement allegations must be struck and considers whether proposed amendments should be allowed.

propositions.text: Gilead proposes two kinds of amendments: one based on Teva's intention to enter market implying stockpiling, another on discovery evidence of admissions.
propositions.quote: The proposed amendments are of two kinds. The first relies on Teva’s stated intention... The second relies on the discovery evidence in Court file T-1529-12

propositions.text: Amendments based on Teva's intention to stockpile are speculative and lack reasonable basis to infer actual stockpiling in Canada.
propositions.quote: the proposed new allegations of the first kind are entirely speculative... there is simply no reasonable basis... to infer that Teva has actually, in Canada, either made or stockpiled commercial quantities

propositions.text: Availability of product is not synonymous with actual possession; prior cases distinguish these concepts in infringement contexts.
propositions.quote: availability is not synonymous with actual possession; taken in context, the word “available” connotes more readily that the product can be obtained than that it is in actual possession

propositions.text: Proposed amendments based on speculation should not be allowed.
propositions.quote: The proposed amendments amount to no more than bald speculation and ought not to be allowed

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Gilead's proposed amendments based on Teva's intention speculative and disallows them, citing prior case law distinguishing availability from possession.

propositions.text: Proposed amendments pleading admissions of infringement mischaracterize discovery evidence and should not be allowed.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the proposed amendments mischaracterize the discovery evidence and that it would accordingly not be in the interest of justice to allow them

propositions.text: Discovery transcript shows Teva admitted only regulatory activities exempted by Patent Act section 55.2.
propositions.quote: Teva has not admitted to any activity beyond the regulatory requirements for the preparation and filing of its ANDS, which are specifically exempted by section 55.2 of the Patent Act

propositions.text: Allegations of conduct exempted by section 55.2 are insufficient to sustain past or current infringement actions.
propositions.quote: It was held in Eli Lilly Canada Inc. et al v Nu-Pharm Inc., 2011 FC 255 that allegations of such conduct are not sufficient to validly sustain an action for past or current infringement

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Gilead's proposed amendments mischaracterize discovery evidence showing only exempt regulatory activities, thus not sustaining infringement claims.

propositions.text: Criteria for valid quia timet patent infringement claim require deliberate intention, imminence, and cogent, precise, material facts.
propositions.quote: the case law generally recognizes and applies the following criteria for validly initiating a quia timet proceeding alleging patent infringement...

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal criteria for a valid quia timet patent infringement claim requiring deliberate intention, imminence, and cogent facts.

propositions.text: Gilead's current claim relies on Teva's expressed intention and procedural circumstances but lacks allegations on Teva's ability to carry out intention.
propositions.quote: Gilead’s statement of claim relies on the allegations made by Teva... but is silent as to Teva’s ability to carry out its professed intention

propositions.text: In a similar case, Novartis met intention but failed temporal imminence criterion due to lack of approvability allegations.
propositions.quote: I held in that case that while Novartis had met the expressed intention criterion, it had failed to meet the temporal aspect of the criteria

propositions.text: Without allegations that Teva's NOC application is approvable and will issue timely, infringement remains speculative.
propositions.quote: Absent allegations to the effect that Teva’s application for an NOC is approvable... the infringement remains speculative

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Gilead's claim lacks allegations on Teva's ability to carry out intention, making infringement speculative like in a prior Novartis case.

propositions.text: Without proposed amendments, Gilead's claim alleges deliberate intention but lacks material facts showing infringement imminence.
propositions.quote: the statement of claim does... allege a deliberate expressed intention... However... lacks sufficient material facts to show that the infringement is imminent

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Gilead's claim alleges intention but lacks material facts to show imminent infringement without amendments.

propositions.text: Discovery evidence and proposed amendments are cogent, precise, and material to satisfy imminence criterion.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the discovery evidence, and the amendments proposed, are sufficiently cogent, precise and material to satisfy the criterion of imminence

propositions.text: Gilead should be allowed to make the proposed amendments.
propositions.quote: Gilead should be allowed to make the proposed amendments

paragraphs.summary: The court finds discovery evidence and proposed amendments satisfy imminence and allows Gilead to amend its claim accordingly.

propositions.text: Gilead argues factual circumstances permit reasonable inference that Teva's submissions are approvable and on patent hold.
propositions.quote: Gilead argued... the following factual circumstances permit a reasonable inference that Teva’s submissions are approvable

propositions.text: The circumstances form a sufficiently cogent, precise, and material set of facts to infer Teva's ANDS is on patent hold.
propositions.quote: those circumstances together... would form a sufficiently cogent, precise and material set of facts from which one could reasonably infer

propositions.text: Even if discovery evidence was disallowed, Gilead could amend to raise these circumstances as material facts.
propositions.quote: Even if I had been wrong in allowing Gilead to rely on the discovery evidence... I would have permitted it to amend to raise the circumstances discussed above

paragraphs.summary: Gilead argues and the court finds factual circumstances support inferring Teva's ANDS is on patent hold; amendments allowed even without discovery evidence.

propositions.text: At pleading stage, plaintiff need only plead a reasonably arguable case, not prove it; motions to strike should not become mini-trials.
propositions.quote: Care must be taken that motions to strike for failure to plead material facts not be turned into a show cause hearing where a plaintiff is required to prove its case

paragraphs.summary: The court states that at pleading stage, a reasonably arguable case suffices and motions to strike should not require proof of the case.

propositions.text: Probability of infringement in July 2017 is sufficiently imminent to justify quia timet action.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the probability that infringement will occur in July 2017 is sufficiently imminent to justify a quia timet action

propositions.text: Quia timet actions aim to prevent events before they happen; initiating 22 months prior is not premature given streamlined proceedings.
propositions.quote: The purpose of a quia timet action is to stop an event before it happens... it is neither premature nor pointless to institute such an action 22 months before

paragraphs.summary: The court finds infringement imminence justifies quia timet action and explains such actions prevent events before they happen, allowing early initiation.

propositions.text: Substantial harm suffices for quia timet claims; irreparable harm is not required; case law offers no further guidance on harm magnitude.
propositions.quote: while allegations of irreparable harm would satisfy that criterion, irreparable harm is not a requirement and allegations of substantial harm will be sufficient

paragraphs.summary: The court states that substantial harm suffices for quia timet claims; irreparable harm is not required and case law lacks further guidance.

propositions.text: Gilead's statement of claim alleges deprivation of exclusivity, damages over $50,000, and Teva's profit.
propositions.quote: The statement of claim currently only alleges that Gilead will be deprived of the statutory exclusivity... that it will suffer damages in excess of $50,000 and that Teva will make a profit

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Gilead's claim alleges loss of exclusivity, damages over $50,000, and Teva's profit.

propositions.text: Deprivation of exclusivity alone does not constitute substantial or irreparable harm for quia timet claims.
propositions.quote: it is clear that it did not contemplate the deprivation of exclusivity rights as constituting, of itself, either irreparable or substantial harm

propositions.text: Infringer's profits do not necessarily constitute harm to patentee regardless of magnitude.
propositions.quote: the profits of an infringer do not necessarily constitute harm to the patentee, whatever their magnitude

propositions.text: Only allegation of damages over $50,000 is imprecise and insufficient to meet substantial harm requirement.
propositions.quote: the only allegation of harm left in Gilead’s statement of claim is that it will suffer damages in excess of $50,000... is, obviously, not precise or cogent enough

propositions.text: Gilead should be allowed to amend to particularize expected damages; Teva may later challenge sufficiency of particulars.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that Gilead should be afforded an opportunity to amend its statement of claim to particularize the monetary loss... with leave to Teva to argue

paragraphs.summary: The court finds exclusivity loss and infringer profits insufficient harm; damages allegation imprecise; allows Gilead to amend damages particulars with Teva's right to challenge.

propositions.text: Gilead is relieved of implied undertaking rule for certain discovery transcripts and should have costs for that motion.
propositions.quote: Gilead has been successful on its motion to be relieved of the implied undertaking rule, and should have its costs of that motion

propositions.text: Gilead's allegations of past or current infringement are struck without leave to amend.
propositions.quote: Gilead’s statement of claim, insofar as it alleges past or current infringement, is hereby struck, without leave to amend

propositions.text: Gilead shall amend its statement of claim to remove past/current infringement allegations and add proposed amendments except specified parts.
propositions.quote: Gilead shall amend its statement of claim to remove allegations of past or current infringement and to add the amendments set out in the proposed amended statement of claim... with exceptions

propositions.text: Gilead shall amend to add particulars of expected damages if Teva enters market before patent expiry.
propositions.quote: Gilead shall also amend its statement of claim to add particulars of the amount of damages it expects to suffer

propositions.text: Teva may reapply to strike claim if particulars fail to allege sufficient material facts of substantial harm.
propositions.quote: Teva shall have leave to reapply to strike the statement of claim on the basis that the particulars to be provided fail to allege sufficient material facts of substantial harm

propositions.text: No costs awarded on Teva's motion to strike as success is divided.
propositions.quote: On Teva’s motion to strike, success being divided, there shall be no costs

paragraphs.summary: The court orders Gilead relieved of implied undertaking rule with costs, strikes past/current infringement claims without leave, allows amendments with exceptions, and no costs on Teva's strike motion.
